notes:
I couldn't find any real Protestant disagreement by denomination on this passage. I found almost nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites, and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Where commentators do disagree (Rachel's motive, verse 42, verse 49, verse 53), the split doesn't follow denominational lines, so I've marked it where it comes up. Nearly all of these notes come from biblehub, studylight, blueletterbible, enduringword, gotquestions and netbible. I ran out of searches before I could check catholic.com, newadvent.org, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org or the denominational sites directly.

**v. 29**
- Ellicott: all ancient translations read this as "it is in the power of my hand." Laban reproaches Jacob, first, for carrying away his daughters secretly, then tells him he would have punished him if God hadn't warned him. Ellicott calls Laban's speech half true and half false, a mix of good and evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Guzik: when Laban's attempt to shame Jacob with kindness failed, Laban threatened Jacob. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
- Matthew Henry: As bad as he was he durst not injure one whom he saw to be the particular care of Heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_031.cfm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God's warning was really of the nature of a rebuke (Genesis 31:42). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**v. 30**
- Guzik: Laban's question shows the foolishness of idolatry. It is sad and strange to have a god that can be stolen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
- Matthew Henry: Enemies may steal our goods, but not our God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_031.cfm
- Utley: the household gods seem to have been superstitiously connected with inheritance and prosperity. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-31.html
- **Why did Rachel take them? (no agreement):** Guzik lists several possible motives: she worshipped them; she wanted to stop Laban using them to find the family; they worked like property deeds; revenge; or, in Jewish tradition, to wean Laban off idolatry (enduringword, above). The Pulpit Commentary adds that some early church fathers held she wanted to draw her father from the practice of idolatry (Bazil, Gregory, Nazisnzen, Theodoret). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-19.htm
- **Modern archaeology:** Constable quotes the view that under the Nuzi tablets he who possessed the household gods was the legitimate heir. But other writers, however, dispute this significance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-20.html

**v. 31**
- Ellicott: Jacob gives the real reason he fled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Utley: Jacob answers Laban's earlier question but not the one about the gods, because he knew nothing of the theft. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-31.html

**v. 32**
- Guzik: Jacob pronounced a harsh curse on the thief without realising he was calling judgment down on his own wife. (Citation fixed below.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
- Ellicott: the answer was as rash as the one Joseph's brothers later gave about the cup. The Rabbins regard this as a prophecy, fulfilled in Rachel's premature death. More simply, it means "I hand him over to you, even to be killed." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html

**vv. 33–34**
- Guzik: Rachel had learned the ways of deception well from her father, and perhaps from her husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
- Ellicott: the teraphim seem to have had human-shaped heads and small bodies, so they would easily fit under the saddle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Barnes: the "camel's saddle" was a pack-saddle, in the recesses of which articles might be deposited. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**v. 35**
- Barnes: Laban accepted her excuse, probably not because of the purity law (Leviticus 15 didn't exist yet) but out of respect for his daughter. He couldn't imagine she would sit on the teraphim in that condition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html
- Clarke: she knew this would satisfy Laban, since a woman in that state was thought to defile what she touched. Pulpit: the phrase "found not," repeated three times, emphasizes the completeness, of Lahan's deception. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-35.html

**vv. 36–37**
- Matthew Henry: Laban pushed even mild Jacob into a temper. His chiding with Laban, though it may admit of some excuse, was not justifiable, nor is it written for our imitation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_031.cfm
- Ellicott: Jacob took the charge about the teraphim as an excuse to search his goods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Utley: the verb for Jacob's challenge has legal connotations. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/genesis-31.html
- Barnes: "my brothers and yours" means their common kindred. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**vv. 38–41**
- Ellicott: from September to May, Eastern nights are cold, and the swing from heat to frost is hard on health. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Ellicott also notes on v. 7 that "ten times" means "a good many times," and he reads v. 41 as possibly two separate 20-year periods (see his excursus on Jacob's timeline). Same URL.
- Preacher's Homiletical: Jacob owed nothing to Laban. He had fairly earned all that he had received. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-35.html

**v. 42**
- "Fear of Isaac." Ellicott says it means the God Isaac worshipped. Jewish commentators explain that Jacob avoided saying "Isaac's God" out of respect, because Isaac was still alive. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Henry/Benson: Abraham was dead, and gone to that world where there is no fear; but Isaac was yet alive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-42.htm
- Gotquestions: the name means Isaac feared God and worshiped Him exclusively. https://www.gotquestions.org/Fear-of-Isaac.html
- **A difference in emphasis (not an open debate):**
  - Clarke (Methodist): Isaac was still on trial in this life, not exempt from the danger of *falling*.
  - Calvin (Reformed): the godly don't fear God with terror like the reprobate. They walk carefully before His judgment.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-42.html
- An excerpt on the biblehub page (commentator not named) says God's ruling condemned Laban without approving everything Jacob had done. Jacob had only met cunning with cunning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-42.htm
- **Modern notes:** NET explains the phrase as the one Isaac feared and respected. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+31%3A42 Coffman, by contrast, uses this verse to argue against the theory that different names for God show different authors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-42.html

**v. 43**
- Ellicott: Laban doesn't answer Jacob's anger. He replies affectionately and suggests a covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Biblical Illustrator, more harshly: Proud oppressors, when they cannot hurt, yet they brag all is theirs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-31.html
- Preacher's Homiletical: The natural feelings of a father prevail. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**vv. 44–46**
- Matthew Henry: Jacob agrees without demanding that Laban give anything back. Better sit down losers than go on in strife. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_031.cfm
- Ellicott: they eat together on the stone mound as a sign of friendship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Barnes: setting up the pillar was a joint act, in which Laban proposes, Jacob performs, and all take part. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**v. 47**
- Ellicott: Jegar-sahadutha is Aramaic (Syriac) and means the same as Galeed, "Heap of Witness." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- Gotquestions: both names mean "witness pile," one in Aramaic, one in Hebrew. https://www.gotquestions.org/Lord-watch-between-you-and-me.html

**v. 48**
- Pulpit: the rocky ground may have suggested the designation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html

**vv. 49–50**
- Mizpah means "watchtower." Ellicott thinks there is a wordplay with *mazzebah*, the Hebrew for "pillar." Laban's use of "Jehovah" shows he and Jacob had talked about religion. https://biblehub.com/genesis/31-49.htm
- Guzik: Mizpah was a warning: "If you do wrong, God will see it and may He punish." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
- Constable: not really a promise between friends but a warning between antagonists who did not trust each other. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html
- Cambridge Bible: the popular use of "Mizpah" ignores the context, and, in particular, Genesis 31:50. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-49.htm
- **Popular modern use (debated):** a biblehub article says Victorians made "Mizpah rings" for separated sweethearts. It treats the shift from warning to blessing as devotional use that still needs careful reading. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_call_Genesis_31_49_Mizpah_Benediction.htm Chuck Smith calls the use as a Christian greeting "tragic." The Biblical Illustrator is gentler: Mizpah tokens can still turn thoughts to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-49.html
- **Modern scholarship:** Cambridge says the name comes in abruptly and may be a gloss. Keil agrees vv. 49–50 look like a later insertion, but says that doesn't prove the story was stitched together from different sources. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-49.htm

**vv. 51–52**
- Biblical Illustrator: Sinful solicitousness for safety is full of words to little purpose (Genesis 31:51). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-31.html
- Guzik, quoting another writer: the pillar meant crossing the line would void the pact (see the enduringword quote above). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/

**v. 53 (commentators genuinely split)**
- **Laban was mixing gods:**
  - Ellicott: the verb "judge" is plural, so Laban apparently thought of Abraham's God and Nahor's god as different. Jacob swears by the one God.
    https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
  - NET: the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek Old Testament changed the verb to singular to make the line monotheistic. Laban was a polytheist, and Nahor's god was probably one of the local deities.
    https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+31:53-54&mode=print
  - Gill (Baptist): each man swore by his own deity.
    https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-53.html
  - Geneva notes: Behold, how the idolaters mingle the true God with their false gods.
    https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-53.htm
  - Poole: Laban was quietly treating Jacob's faith as a novelty, which teaches that antiquity of itself is no certain argument of the true church.
    https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-53.htm
- **Laban meant the one true God:**
  - Matthew Henry: the wording shows that they worshipped one and the same God.
    https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/31-53.html
  - Barnes: it shows Terah's line still acknowledged the true God even in their idolatry.
    https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-53.htm

**v. 54**
- Ellicott: Jacob killed animals and held a feast. Animals were originally killed only for sacrifice, so Hebrew uses one word for both. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html
- NET: probably a kind of peace offering, where the person bringing it ate the meat. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+31:53-54&mode=print
- Barnes: The common sacrifice and the common meal ratify the covenant of reconciliation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-53.htm

**v. 55**
- Matthew Henry (Concise): After this angry parley, they part friends. God is often better to us than our fears. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/31-53.htm
- Ellicott (on v. 28) and Guzik both note that Laban's "sons" here means his grandsons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-31.html

*Correction to v. 32:* the Guzik quote should be cited to the full enduringword page I opened. He says Jacob pronounced a harsh curse on the thief, not knowing that he actually invited judgment on his own wife. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-31/
